rationales: Solids do not move randomly from place to place; their particles remain in fixed positions.
Solid molecules vibrate about their mean positions.
Rotational motion is not the characteristic motion of molecules in a solid.
Molecules in a solid do not travel from the hot end to the cold end.
Gas molecules do not move only in one straight line; they change direction in collisions.
Gas molecules move randomly, traveling in different directions between collisions.
Gas molecules are not limited to vibratory motion about fixed positions.
Gas molecules are not limited to rotational motion.
Temperature is not the total amount of heat in a substance.
Temperature does not measure how many molecules a substance contains.
Temperature indicates the degree of hotness or coldness of a substance.
Temperature is not defined by the distance between molecules.
Heat is not the total kinetic energy of the molecules; that is related to a substance’s internal energy.
Heat is not simply the internal energy stored in a substance.
Work done by molecules is not the definition of heat.
Heat is energy transferred from one body to another because of a temperature difference.
Zero kelvin is absolute zero, not the melting point of ice.
32 is the melting point of ice in degrees Fahrenheit, not kelvins.
−273°C is approximately absolute zero, not the melting point of ice.
The melting point of ice is approximately +273 K.
−40 has the same numerical value on the Celsius and Fahrenheit scales.
+40°C and +40°F are different temperatures.
+45°C and +45°F are different temperatures.
−45°C and −45°F are different temperatures.
Being colourless makes a liquid harder to see in the thermometer tube.
Being a bad conductor is not the key property that ensures accurate liquid expansion readings.
A suitable thermometric liquid should expand uniformly, or nearly linearly, with temperature.
A liquid that wets the glass can leave a film and make the reading less reliable.
Alcohol’s large expansivity is generally an advantage because it makes temperature changes easier to detect.
Alcohol’s low freezing point is an advantage for measuring low temperatures.
Alcohol wets the glass, which can make the thermometer reading less reliable.
Alcohol’s approximately linear expansion is an advantage for a thermometric liquid.
Water’s lack of colour is inconvenient but is not the main reason it is unsuitable.
Water’s relatively poor thermal conductivity is not the main limitation cited for its use in thermometers.
Water expands non-linearly over a range of temperatures, making its scale unreliable.
A boiling point of 100°C limits the range but is not the main reason given here.
A narrow capillary does not by itself make the thermometer respond more quickly to temperature changes.
A narrow capillary does not allow a thermometer to record the maximum temperature.
A narrow capillary makes a small volume expansion produce a larger visible movement of the liquid column.
A narrow capillary does not increase the thermometer’s measurable temperature range.
A thermocouple thermometer responds quickly and is well suited to rapidly varying temperatures.
A mercury-in-glass laboratory thermometer responds more slowly than a thermocouple.
An alcohol-in-glass thermometer is not as suitable as a thermocouple for rapidly changing temperatures.
A clinical thermometer is designed for body-temperature measurement, not rapid temperature variations.
